name: Villanueva v. California
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California)
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force; shooting into a slowly moving pickup truck after a pursuit; vehicle as a weapon; passenger as a seized person; qualified immunity denied
summary: Two plainclothes officers in an unmarked car followed a pickup truck from an illegal street sideshow through a high speed drive that ended on a dead end street. When the truck made a slow three point turn with its front generally facing the officers 15 to 20 feet away, both officers fired, killing the driver and wounding the passenger. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity. Taking the facts in the plaintiffs' favor, the truck was moving very slowly, was not aimed at either officer, and was not accelerating, so the officers could have stepped aside; Acosta v. City and County of San Francisco had clearly established since 1996 that shooting at a slow moving car an officer can step out of the way of is unreasonable. The court also held the passenger was seized when officers fired to stop the truck. It is taught for what the Ninth Circuit says about vehicles as weapons.
coverage: The full opinion by Judge Wardlaw, joined by Judge Ebel of the Tenth Circuit sitting by designation and Judge Owens, including all footnotes, was read from https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/01/28/19-55225.pdf. The slip opinion is headed No. 19-55225, D.C. No. 8:17-cv-01302-JLS-KES, submitted May 14, 2020 (decided without oral argument), filed January 28, 2021, and marked for publication. The running head is Villanueva v. Cleveland; the caption lists the State of California as defendant and Cleveland and Henderson as defendants appellants.
The reporter citation 986 F.3d 1158 was supplied in the assignment and was not confirmed from the slip opinion, which carries no reporter pagination. No pin cites to the F.3d are given.

The opinion identifies the officers as Sergeant Cleveland and Officer Henderson, represented by the California Attorney General, and refers to them as police officers. The opinion does not name their agency, and this brief does not either.
Acosta v. City and County of San Francisco, Orn v. City of Tacoma, Wilkinson v. Torres, and Monzon v. City of Murrieta were not read; they are described as the Villanueva court described them.

The opinion arose on interlocutory appeal from the denial of summary judgment, with the facts stated in the plaintiffs' favor and many facts disputed. No later proceedings in the district court were verified.
The appeals as to the passenger's false detention and arrest claims were dismissed because the officers had not asserted qualified immunity on those claims in the district court.

Citation as written in the brief: 986 F.3d 1158 (9th Cir. 2021). The source read gave it as: 986 F.3d 1158 (9th Cir. 2021) (reporter cite as supplied in course materials; not confirmed from the slip opinion).
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit recounted them in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs; many were disputed. On July 3, 2016, at about 10:35 p.m., Sergeant Cleveland and Officer Henderson were on patrol near Fullerton, California, looking for illegal street racing and sideshows. They wore plain clothes and dark tactical vests with police insignia and drove an unmarked black sedan equipped with red and blue and blue and amber lights. They found a sideshow of about twenty cars in a swap meet parking lot. A red Chevrolet Silverado driven by Pedro Villanueva with Francisco Orozco as passenger performed or attempted an illegal maneuver, and the officers drove in to make a traffic stop.

As they entered, the Silverado drove toward the exit. The officers followed. According to Orozco, they used only an amber light and a screeching sound not identifiable as a police siren, and the truck left the lot at a speed that did not feel fast. The officers then turned off their lights and siren and followed. Villanueva and Orozco said they were scared because they had been warned about muggers in black sedans at truck events. Villanueva drove 50 to 70 miles per hour on surface streets and ran at least three red lights; the officers followed at a disputed distance, using their siren intermittently at intersections. After several minutes Villanueva turned onto one dead end street and then another, where the truck stopped.

The officers got out of their car immediately and drew their firearms, Cleveland by the open driver's door and Henderson by the open passenger door. Villanueva attempted to reverse out of the dead end with a three point turn that left the rear of the truck pointing toward one dead end and the front generally facing the officers, who were 15 to 20 feet away. The officers opened fire and shouted some warning at the same time or within a second of firing. The shots killed Villanueva and wounded Orozco. The truck then rolled slowly forward and collided with the police car at very low speed.

The officers said Villanueva drove recklessly during the turn, hit a car behind him, faced them, and hit the gas before they fired. Orozco said the turn was below the speed limit, that the truck did not hit another vehicle, that it was not moving directly toward the police car, and that he never saw either officer in its path. Three independent witnesses testified that the turn was slow and controlled and that they heard no engine revving, tire screeching, or collision and saw no acceleration toward the officers. Orozco was detained in the truck until a supervisor arrived, then handcuffed and taken to a hospital.

Orozco and Villanueva's parents sued for excessive force and other claims. The district court denied summary judgment on qualified immunity for the excessive force claims, finding too many disputes of material fact and that a jury could find a violation of clearly established law. The officers appealed.
holding:
Affirmed as to the excessive force claims; appeals dismissed as to the passenger's detention and arrest claims; remanded.

The passenger was seized. The officers argued it was not clearly established that a passenger struck by a bullet intended for the driver can bring a Fourth Amendment claim because they subjectively intended to shoot only Villanueva. The court rejected the argument. A seizure occurs when freedom of movement is terminated through means intentionally applied (Brower), and the test is objective: it asks what a reasonable passenger would understand, not what the officers intended (Brendlin). Officers who shoot at a vehicle to stop it seize everyone in it, just as a roadblock would, and it does not matter whether they knew a passenger was present. The Ninth Circuit had already applied those principles in Nelson v. City of Davis, where officers who fired pepperballs into a crowd seized the student they hit, and every other circuit to address a passenger struck by a bullet aimed at a vehicle agreed. Orozco was seized under clearly established law.

The standard for vehicles. Deadly force against a fleeing suspect is permitted only if the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a threat of serious physical harm to the officer or others (Garner, Orn). "A moving vehicle can of course pose a threat of serious physical harm, but only if someone is at risk of being struck by it." Deadly force to stop a recklessly speeding vehicle during a chase is therefore ordinarily reasonable (Mullenix, Scott v. Harris, Plumhoff). But this was not a shooting during a high speed chase: it was undisputed that Villanueva had slowed below the speed limit, stopped on the dead end street, and then made the three point turn, and even on the officers' account the truck was moving at up to five miles per hour when they fired. The Ninth Circuit has consistently found deadly force against a slow moving vehicle unreasonable when the officers could easily have stepped out of its path (Acosta, Orn), and has found it reasonable against a stopped or slow moving vehicle only when the driver was trying to escape aggressively through attempted or actual acceleration (Monzon, where the accelerator was pressed 80 to 99 percent and the van reached 17 miles per hour; Wilkinson, where a minivan was accelerating in a slippery yard around an officer who had fallen; Plumhoff). The key question was therefore whether Villanueva accelerated or attempted to accelerate toward the officers before they fired.

Application. The officers' argument rested entirely on their fear that the truck was about to hit Cleveland; they did not claim probable cause of a violent crime, and they had observed only traffic violations. The witnesses' testimony contradicted the officers' account of reckless driving, a collision, and acceleration. Taking the facts in the plaintiffs' favor, the three point turn was performed cautiously, the truck 15 to 20 feet away was not aimed directly at Cleveland, and it was moving very slowly and not accelerating when the shooting began. A reasonable jury could find excessive force because the officers lacked an objectively reasonable basis to fear for their safety when they could simply have stepped back or to the side.

Clearly established. Acosta, decided in 1996, held that an officer who shot the driver of a car rolling very slowly from a standstill toward him violated the Fourth Amendment, because a reasonable officer would have recognized he could avoid injury by stepping to the side. Orn, decided in 2020 on facts from an earlier incident, reaffirmed that Acosta clearly established that shooting at a slow moving vehicle the officer could sidestep is unreasonable. The facts here, taken in the plaintiffs' favor, were not fairly distinguishable from Acosta: the vehicle had been stopped shortly before, no officer stood directly in front of it, and the driver did not accelerate toward the officers before they fired. Wilkinson did not undermine Acosta because it involved a revving, mud bound van that could gain traction at any moment and an officer on the ground. The officers' disputed claim that Villanueva hit the gas could not support qualified immunity at the summary judgment stage. The court stressed that what the officers most forcefully contested was whether their account of the shooting should be accepted, which is a question for the jury, not for an interlocutory appeal.
notDecided:
Whether the officers in fact used excessive force. The court held only that a jury could so find on the plaintiffs' version of disputed facts. If a jury accepts the officers' account that the truck accelerated toward them, the analysis could be different.

Whether the pursuit itself, the use of an unmarked car, or the officers' decision to exit and draw weapons was reasonable. The case was decided on the shooting alone.

Whether the officers were entitled to qualified immunity on Orozco's false detention and arrest claims. The officers did not assert the defense in the district court, and the court held it waived for purposes of the appeal.

Any state law claim. The opinion addresses only the Fourth Amendment claims.

Whether shooting at a vehicle that is accelerating toward an officer is reasonable. The court described Monzon, Wilkinson, and Plumhoff as cases where such force was reasonable, but it did not have that fact pattern before it.
inPractice:
Villanueva states the Ninth Circuit's rule on vehicles as weapons in one sentence: a moving vehicle can pose a threat of serious physical harm, but only if someone is at risk of being struck by it. The court then drew the line it has drawn in a series of cases. Shooting to stop a recklessly speeding car in a chase is ordinarily reasonable. Shooting at a stopped or slow moving car is reasonable when the driver is aggressively trying to escape by accelerating or attempting to accelerate toward or around officers. Shooting at a slow moving car that an officer could simply step away from is unreasonable, and has been clearly established as unreasonable in the Ninth Circuit since Acosta in 1996.

The second lesson is about proof. The officers said the truck hit a car, faced them, and accelerated. The passenger and three independent witnesses said the turn was slow and controlled with no revving or screeching. On an interlocutory appeal the court had to take the witnesses' version, and under that version the officers lost. The court said plainly that what the officers most forcefully contested was whether their account should be believed, which is a jury question. An officer who shoots at a vehicle should expect the speed, direction, acceleration, and his own position relative to the car's path to be reconstructed from every available witness and from physical evidence.

The third lesson concerns passengers. Firing at a car to stop it seizes everyone in it, whether or not the officer knows they are there or intends to hit them. A passenger struck by a round meant for the driver has a Fourth Amendment claim.

Dr. Sowards teaches Villanueva in the deadly force line for the vehicle as weapon analysis. The training point is positional: an officer who is not in the path of a slowly moving vehicle, or who can step out of it, generally cannot justify deadly force by the vehicle alone, and department policies that restrict shooting at moving vehicles track this case law.
trainIt:
Teach the three categories the court used. Put them on the board with the cases: a recklessly speeding car in a chase (Scott v. Harris, Plumhoff, Mullenix), a stopped or slow car whose driver is accelerating or attempting to accelerate toward or around officers (Monzon, Wilkinson), and a slow moving car an officer can step away from (Acosta, Orn, Villanueva). Have students sort scenarios into the categories and articulate the facts that move a case from one to another: speed, acceleration, direction relative to the officer, the officer's ability to move, and whether anyone else is in the path.

Teach positioning at vehicle stops and at the end of pursuits. In Villanueva the officers stood beside the open doors of their car 15 to 20 feet in front of a truck that was turning around. Have students plan where to be when a pursued vehicle stops at a dead end: behind cover, out of the vehicle's likely path, with a plan for the car to move again. The court's point was that an officer who can step aside has a reasonable alternative to shooting, and the Ninth Circuit treats that as settled law.

Teach the warning. The officers shouted a warning at the same time as or within a second of firing. Garner and Ninth Circuit cases treat a feasible warning as part of reasonableness. Train students to give commands before force when time allows and to understand that a warning simultaneous with the shot will not be credited as a warning.

Teach the evidence. Three uninvolved witnesses contradicted the officers on revving, screeching, collision, and acceleration. Teach students to document their position, the vehicle's movement, and what they perceived, and to understand that the physical scene, vehicle data, and witnesses will be compared with their account.

Teach the passenger rule. Everyone in the car is seized when an officer fires to stop it. The consequences of a round fired at a vehicle extend to everyone inside and beyond it.

The decision is an interlocutory ruling affirming the denial of summary judgment; the facts are the plaintiffs' version and many were disputed, and the court did not find that the officers used excessive force. applications.title: A vehicle is a weapon only if someone is in its path
applications.body: The court said a moving vehicle can pose a threat of serious physical harm, but only if someone is at risk of being struck by it. If the officer can step aside from a slow moving car, the car alone does not justify deadly force.

applications.title: Acceleration is the dividing line
applications.body: Deadly force against a stopped or slow vehicle has been upheld when the driver was accelerating or attempting to accelerate toward or around officers. The key question here was whether the truck accelerated before the shots; the plaintiffs' witnesses said it did not.

applications.title: Clearly established since 1996
applications.body: Acosta held that shooting the driver of a car rolling slowly toward an officer who could step to the side violates the Fourth Amendment. Orn and Villanueva treat that rule as settled law in the Ninth Circuit.

applications.title: Everyone in the car is seized
applications.body: Firing at a vehicle to stop it seizes the driver and every passenger, whether or not the officer knows they are there or intends to hit them. A passenger struck by a round has a Fourth Amendment claim.

applications.title: Your account will be tested
applications.body: The officers said the truck accelerated; the passenger and three bystanders said it did not. On appeal the court took the witnesses' version. Position, speed, direction, and the timing of any warning will be reconstructed from all the evidence.

quiz.q: According to Villanueva, when does a moving vehicle pose a threat of serious physical harm that can justify deadly force?
options: Whenever the driver has fled from police
Only if someone is at risk of being struck by it
Whenever the vehicle is facing an officer
quiz.teach: The court quoted Orn for that rule and held that a slow moving truck that was not aimed at the officers and was not accelerating, when the officers could step aside, did not justify shooting.

quiz.q: Which case did the court hold clearly established the unlawfulness of the shooting, and as of when?
options: Acosta v. City and County of San Francisco, 1996
quiz.teach: Acosta held that an officer who shot the driver of a slowly rolling car he could have sidestepped violated the Fourth Amendment. Orn reaffirmed it, and the court found the facts here not fairly distinguishable.

quiz.q: What did the court hold about the passenger, Orozco, who was wounded by shots aimed at the truck?
options: He had no Fourth Amendment claim because the officers did not intend to shoot him
He had a claim only under state law
He was seized under clearly established law because the officers intentionally fired at the vehicle to stop it, regardless of whether they knew he was there
His claim depended on whether he was a licensed driver
quiz.teach: Under Brower, Brendlin, and Nelson v. City of Davis, firing at a vehicle to stop it is an intentional application of force that seizes everyone inside. The officers' subjective intent and knowledge were irrelevant.
